messages.content: I'm planning a camping trip and I need to know the weather forecast. Can you fetch me the weather data for the campsite located at latitude 35.68 and longitude -121.34 for the next 10 days including daily temperature and precipitation forecasts? Also, I prefer the temperature 2 minute max in Fahrenheit and sum of precipitation in inches.

function.name: requests_get
function.description: Sends a GET request to the specified URL and retrieves data as specified by the parameters. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

url.description: The URL to which the GET request is sent. It is expected to be a well-formed HTTP or HTTPS URL.

Content-Type.description: The MIME type of the body of the request (used with POST and PUT requests).

Accept.description: The Media type(s) that is/are acceptable for the response.

headers.description: A dictionary of HTTP headers to send with the request. Each key-value pair represents a header name and its value.

timeout.description: The number of seconds to wait for the server to send data before giving up, as a float, or a (connect_timeout, read_timeout) tuple. This is a float type value.

lat.description: Latitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

lon.description: Longitude of the location for the query, in degrees. This is a float type value.

params.description: Query parameters to append to the URL for the GET request.

allow_redirects.description: Determines if HTTP redirections (301, 302, etc.) should be followed.

auth.description: A tuple representing the user credentials for HTTP authentication, typically in the form of (username, password).

cert.description: Path to an SSL certificate file to verify the peer, or a tuple of (certificate file, key file).

cookies.description: A dictionary of cookies to send with the request. The key is the cookie name and the value is the cookie value.

http.description: URL of the proxy for HTTP requests.

https.description: URL of the proxy for HTTPS requests.

proxies.description: A dictionary mapping protocol names to the URL of the proxy.

stream.description: If True, the response content will not be downloaded immediately but streamed.

verify.description: Whether to verify the server's TLS certificate or not, or a path to a CA bundle if verification is needed.

message.reasoning:
We need to use the tool `requests_get` to get weather data from some API. We have no direct knowledge of what endpoint to call; we can guess maybe open-meteo.com or other free APIs.

The prompt says "fetch me the weather data ... for the next 10 days". So likely using open-meteo.com API: e.g., https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast?latitude=...&longitude=...&daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum&timezone=auto&start_date=&end_date=. But they want 10 days ahead inclusive. We'll compute start_date today, end_date +9 days.

But we don't have current date inside environment. Could approximate via today's date. Let's assume it's 2026-05-18. Then start_date=2026-05-19? Actually "next 10 days" might include tomorrow through day after 9 days. Use start_date=today+1? Or just start_date=today? Might choose start_date=2026-05-18. Provide 10-day forecast starting now.

We'll produce JSON output summarizing each day's high temp and precip sum.

Let's craft the request:

URL: https://api.open-meteo.com/v1/forecast

Params:
lat=35.68
lon=-121.34
daily=temperature_2m_max,precipitation_sum
timezone=America/Los_Angeles (or auto)
format=json
start_date=2026-05-18
end_date=2026-05-27

Also specify units: Temperature unit automatically returns Celsius unless set parameter ?units=imperial? For open-meteo, there is param "temperature_unit=celsius|fahrenheit"? Actually open-meteo uses "temperature_unit": "celsius", "windspeed_unit":"kmh","precipitation_unit":"mm". There's also "hourly_units" etc. There may be "temperature_unit=fahrenheit".

Alternatively we could convert ourselves later.

Better approach: Request with "temperature_unit=fahrenheit" and "precipitation_unit=inches". According to docs, open-meteo supports "precipitation_unit=inch"?? Not sure. Maybe easier to keep defaults then convert manually.

Given limited time, I'll ask the tool to retrieve raw data and then process conversion.

So first step: make GET request to open-meteo API.

Use function calls accordingly.

Then parse result into list of dicts per day.

Compute conversions: Celsius to Fahrenheit: F=(C*9/5)+32. Precip mm to inches: inch=mm /25.4.

Return summary table.

Ok let's do it.
